column2: Soil: up to 72,000 mg/kg (Stockpile 3, 2006 SI); single 2012 boring 130,000 mg/kg; site-wide 95% UCL 7,556 mg/kg. Groundwater: 40–370 µg/L across all wells 2012–2023
column3: Soil residential CHHSL 5,200 mg/kg; industrial CHHSL 63,000 mg/kg. Groundwater MCL 1,000 µg/L
column4: Cardiovascular — disrupts potassium balance, affecting heart rhythm and blood pressure; not classified as a carcinogen
column5: Direct ingestion or inhalation of disturbed stockpile soil; barium sulfate (barite) is low solubility which limits leaching, but mechanically disturbed dust poses an inhalation and ingestion hazard
column6: Pre-cap (2004–2019): surface runoff from exposed, unvegetated stockpile surfaces could transport barium-bearing soil particles to adjacent drainage. One isolated stormwater sample near Stockpile 3 measured 2,000 µg/L (2× MCL). Groundwater remained below MCL throughout 9 years of monitoring — barite form resists leaching
column7: Pre-cap: wind erosion of unprotected stockpile surfaces was a plausible pathway for barium-bearing dust to adjacent properties; 2012 fenceline/perimeter samples found barium at 34–4,300 mg/kg at surface — consistent with some historical dust dispersal. Post-cap (2020+): controlled by clean-fill cap and SR-132 pavement
column8: Containment remedy approved 2018; soil consolidated and capped as SR-132 highway embankment fill 2019–2020; Land Use Covenant recorded April 2024 confirms 72,000 mg/kg remains in place under cap; permanent deed restriction bars residential use

column2: Soil: 12–34 mg/kg in stockpile perimeter surfaces; up to 100 mg/kg in SR-99 shoulder surface soil (ADL survey, 2012). Groundwater: non-detect to ~8 µg/L
column3: Soil residential CHHSL 80 mg/kg (CalEPA) — SR-99 ADL exceeded this. Water MCL 15 µg/L — never exceeded in any well
column4: Neurological — no safe blood lead level (CDC/WHO); children especially vulnerable; low-level exposure linked to reduced IQ, attention deficits, and behavioral effects
column5: Direct ingestion or hand-to-mouth contact with surface soil by children; ingestion of homegrown produce grown in lead-contaminated soil near the SR-99/SR-132 corridor
column6: Below MCL in all groundwater wells throughout monitoring (max ~8 µg/L vs. 15 µg/L); lead is relatively immobile in near-neutral soil pH; not a primary historical water pathway
column7: Primary historical dispersal mechanism: decades of leaded-gasoline exhaust aerially deposited lead along the SR-99/SR-132 corridor (1930s–1996 phaseout); settled lead persists in surface soils of adjacent neighborhoods within ~100–150m of the roadway — this historical deposition is independent of and predates the stockpile remediation
column8: ADL from historic vehicle exhaust is the dominant source; ADL soil from SR-99 shoulder co-remediated with barium containment fill 2019–2020; neighborhood surface soils near the corridor may retain legacy lead at elevated concentrations not addressed by the Caltrans remediation scope

column2: 2004 PSI: anomalous "elevated" readings co-located with extreme barium (judged lab false positives). 2006 + 2012 retesting (348 samples): all non-detect. Isolated 2012 confirmations: 0.26–0.78 mg/kg across stockpiles
column3: Soil residential CHHSL 1.7 mg/kg; industrial CHHSL 7.5 mg/kg — none exceeded in reliable testing
column4: IARC Group 1 carcinogen; accumulates irreversibly in kidneys over decades; can cause renal failure; lung damage via inhalation
column5: Ingestion of contaminated soil (hand-to-mouth); consumption of crops grown in contaminated soil — plants concentrate cadmium readily; occupational inhalation of dust
column6: No significant groundwater detections documented; moderately mobile under acidic conditions but no evidence of aquifer impact at this site
column7: Inhaled cadmium particles or dust can cause lung damage and increase cancer risk; minimal pathway here given confirmed near-background concentrations
column8: 2004 detections were lab false positives due to spectral interference from co-located extreme barium concentrations (different lab than later rounds); 348-sample retest found nothing; only low-level 2012 confirmations well below CHHSLs; cadmium was not confirmed as a site contaminant of concern

column2: Groundwater: 1.3–18 µg/L across all wells and events 2012–2019; soil slightly above background in some samples but never above CHHSL
column3: Water MCL 50 µg/L (max detected 18 µg/L, 36% of limit). No soil CHHSL exceeded
column4: Hexavalent chromium (Cr-VI) is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen via inhalation (the "Erin Brockovich" chemical); trivalent chromium (Cr-III) is far less toxic; speciation at this site is unknown
column5: Ingestion of contaminated groundwater if used as drinking water source; inhalation of Cr-VI dust during soil disturbance
column6: Limited historical water dispersal; max 18 µg/L well below MCL throughout all monitoring; not a significant groundwater pathway historically or currently
column7: Low historical air dispersal; soil chromium was near background; Cr-VI airborne dust from smelting/welding operations is the primary industrial air pathway but not documented at this site
column8: Total chromium only reported — hexavalent/trivalent speciation not available; never confirmed above a soil CHHSL; never a driver of site risk assessment

column2: One Stockpile 2 boring (2012): diesel-range TPH 120 mg/kg; motor-oil-range TPH 82 mg/kg; three PAHs (2-methylnaphthalene, fluorene, phenanthrene) at 23–45 µg/kg. Gasoline-range: not detected
column3: Leaching-based threshold: 83 mg/kg (diesel-range exceeded). Direct-contact residential 110 mg/kg / industrial 450 mg/kg — not exceeded. PAH screening levels not approached
column4: Liver, kidney, and nervous system effects with prolonged exposure; benzo(a)pyrene (when present) is a proven human carcinogen; diesel-range compounds are potential endocrine disruptors
column5: Inhalation of vapor or dust during soil disturbance; dermal contact with contaminated soil; incidental ingestion (hand-to-mouth)
column6: Low water solubility for diesel-range compounds; no groundwater impacts documented; lighter (gasoline-range) fractions that could leach more readily were not detected
column7: Volatile lighter fractions (gasoline-range) are the primary air dispersal pathway for petroleum sites — not detected here; diesel-range is far less volatile; limited historical air dispersal at this site based on available data
column8: Single confirmed detection from one boring analyzed on the basis of field odor and staining in 2012; motor-oil-range and all PAHs below direct-exposure thresholds; not treated as a driver of site risk; no documented landfill disposal of PAH-contaminated material in the reviewed record

column2: Groundwater: MW-5 (downgradient) 20–30 mg/L, 2012–2013; MW-1 (upgradient/background) 12–13 mg/L; multiple wells exceeded MCL sporadically through 2012–2019
column3: MCL 10 mg/L (drinking water health standard — set to protect infants)
column4: Converts to nitrite in the body, impairing blood oxygen-carrying capacity; causes methemoglobinemia ("blue baby syndrome") — potentially fatal in infants under 6 months; low toxicity in adults at these concentrations
column5: Ingestion of contaminated well water, especially by formula-fed infants; private groundwater wells in the region are the primary risk pathway
column6: Primary pathway — historically and currently: decades of Central Valley agricultural fertilizer and irrigation have contaminated the regional aquifer; nitrate migrates laterally through the aquifer over large distances; this is a regional condition, not site-specific
column7: Not a significant air dispersal pathway
column8: Upgradient well MW-1 (outside any stockpile influence) also exceeds the MCL at 12–13 mg/L, confirming regional agricultural background, not stockpile-caused contamination; this groundwater is not a drinking water source at the site; municipal supply in the area uses treated water

column2: Groundwater: up to 260 µg/L (MW-1 and MW-7, March 2013); sporadically exceeded secondary MCL in nearly every well at some point 2012–2019
column3: Secondary MCL 50 µg/L — aesthetic standard only (taste, odor, staining); no primary health-based MCL for manganese in drinking water
column4: Secondary MCL protects against taste, odor, and staining — not a toxicological standard; high occupational inhaled exposure (e.g., welding fumes, far above any drinking-water scenario) can cause "manganism," a neurological movement disorder; no established health risk at concentrations seen here
column5: Aesthetic concern in drinking water (metallic taste, black/brown staining); occupational inhalation in industrial settings (welding, mining) — not relevant here
column6: Naturally present throughout the monitoring network with no spatial pattern attributable to the stockpiles; widespread in Central Valley alluvial groundwater due to local geology; historically a background condition
column7: Not a significant air dispersal pathway at this site
column8: No remediation required or proposed; no spatial concentration pattern linked to the stockpiles; naturally abundant in Central Valley alluvial deposits; monitoring wells decommissioned 2019–2023 as they went dry; recommended for monitoring discontinuation February 2023

column2: Soil (Stockpile 2 surface, 2006, 33 samples): 0.7–4.9 mg/kg, 95% UCL 1.63 mg/kg. Soil (all stockpiles, all depths, 165 samples): up to 14 mg/kg. Groundwater: 1.3–6.6 µg/L across all wells 2012–2019
column3: Soil residential RSL 0.39 mg/kg; residential CHHSL 0.07 mg/kg (both far below background). Water MCL 10 µg/L — groundwater never exceeded
column4: Cancer (IARC Group 1); arsenic in Stockpile 2 surface soil alone produced a calculated cancer risk of 1.45E-5 — 10x above the standard 1E-6 threshold — and drove the total SP2 cancer risk estimate to 1E-5 in the 2007 HHRA, before background adjustment
column5: Ingestion of or dermal contact with surface soil, especially by children (off-site resident/trespasser scenario); arsenic's soil screening levels are so low (0.07-0.39 mg/kg) that even natural background soil exceeds them
column6: No significant groundwater pathway — arsenic stayed at 13-66% of MCL in all wells/events; not a driver of any water-based risk
column7: Historical wind erosion/dust from exposed stockpile surfaces (pre-cap, 2004-2019) could have distributed background-level arsenic-bearing soil, same as barium and lead, though arsenic itself is not elevated above regional background
column8: CRITICAL CONTEXT: this was a false alarm from natural background, not stockpile contamination. Local background soil (adjacent Caltrans property) measured 0.2–4.1 mg/kg — nearly identical to the 0.7–4.9 mg/kg found on Stockpile 2. When background 95% UCL (1.15 mg/kg) is used as the exposure point concentration instead of the site value, the calculated cancer risk is 1.15E-5 — statistically indistinguishable from the site's 1.45E-5. DTSC/HHRA excluded arsenic as a chemical of concern (COC) on this basis; after removing its contribution, the Stockpile 2 total cancer risk estimate dropped from 1E-5 to 1E-7 (below threshold). Source: 2007 Shaw HHRA, reproduced in Geocon's Dec 2012/Mar 2013 HHRA Update
